steps: Predict the downstream data-product decision before executing.

Classify every column: Each column gets a sensitivity class. pii_direct identifies a person outright (email); pii_quasi re-identifies in combination (ZIP). No column is left without a class — that is the whole invariant.
Direct PII → mask: email is pii_direct, so its policy is mask (irreversible hash). A metric never needs the raw value — only whether two rows share one.
Quasi-identifier → tokenize: home_zip alone is not a name, but ZIP + age + gender re-identifies. Tokenize into a k-anonymity bucket so the analytic value survives and the person does not.
The gate detects drift: When the source team adds a column tomorrow, source_cols has it but the contract does not — unclassified is non-empty. This is the SELECT * leak, caught.
Fail the build, do not warn: raise, not log. A warning is ignored at 2 a.m.; a raised GovernanceError stops the run and quarantines the batch before it reaches the mart.
Emit the enforced plan: The gate returns the policy per column — the plan dbt applies and lineage carries. This plan IS the reviewable evidence: policy that runs, not policy that's promised.

storyboard.say: It starts at the source: raw_users hands its columns to a source contract that must declare what each column actually is.
The contract feeds the governance gate, whose only job is to check that every column carries a sensitivity class.
Here is the failure path: a column has no class, so an ungoverned SELECT star copies it straight through, untouched.
That raw copy carries raw_email and home ZIP into a dashboard three teams can query — the Monday-morning leak.
Now the repair path: because the column is classified, the gate routes it to policy, which masks the sensitive value.
Governed rows land in the warehouse, and the PII tag rides the lineage forward into the dbt model.
The tag reaches the served metric safely — the invariant holds: no unclassified column ever reaches a mart.
The lesson: policy that isn't enforced at the gate is decoration; a tag that travels with the data is protection.

privacy-governance.text: DORA 2024 does not state that elite teams treat governance as a build gate; that is not a DORA finding. Rephrase without DORA attribution: 'Treat governance as a build gate, not a review meeting — the same discipline that makes deploys safe makes data safe.' The senior tell is column-level lineage: not "this table has PII" but "this metric is derived from email, masked here, and here is the query that proves the raw value never left staging." A reviewer trusts the tag they can trace, not the promise they're told.

privacy-governance.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this pipeline is governed, not just documented." Which response actually proves it?
options: "Our data-handling policy page says all PII is protected and the team is trained."

"Column-level lineage shows email is classed pii_direct, masked in staging, and the query proves the raw value never reaches the mart — plus a quarantine report where the gate BLOCKED an unclassified column last week."
"All our dbt tests pass and the metric matches the source count."
"We use SELECT * so we never miss a column, and the warehouse is access-controlled."
privacy-governance.explanation: Only option 2 points to enforced, traceable evidence: a column-level classification, the policy applied, lineage proving the raw value never propagated, AND a real quarantine event showing the gate stops the failure. Option 1 is prose (the leak path). Option 3 proves correctness, not privacy — a metric can be exactly right and still expose raw email. Option 4 is the exact anti-pattern: SELECT * is how unclassified columns leak, and table-level access control does not govern which columns flow downstream.

observability-alerting.doNotClaim: Do not claim a pipeline is observable because it 'has logs' or 'has a dashboard'. A dashboard nobody watches at 3 a.m. is not observability. Observability means a specific signal crosses a specific threshold and pages a specific human with a specific next action — or it does not exist.

observability-alerting.text: The exec dashboard read $4.1M in revenue for six days before anyone noticed the source feed had gone stale on day one — the warehouse kept serving yesterday's partition, dbt kept building green, and the metric quietly lied to the board. No test failed, because nobody was watching freshness.

This lesson is the synthesis capstone of the module: it sits on top of source contracts, ingestion, dbt models, quality, lineage, and reconciliation. Observability is the layer that turns all of those into signals that page a human before a stale or malformed partition corrupts a downstream metric.

observability-alerting.prompt: Your dbt run is green, tests pass, and the dashboard renders. Is the pipeline healthy? Answer before reading on.
observability-alerting.reveal: Not necessarily — green means the code ran, not that the data is true. dbt builds happily on a source that stopped updating three days ago: the partition is present, the schema matches, tests on shape pass. The one signal that catches this is freshness — max(loaded_at) vs now — and it is exactly the signal most pipelines never alert on. 'Green build' measures the pipeline; observability measures the data flowing through it.

observability-alerting.code:
sources:
  - name: orders_raw
    loaded_at_field: loaded_at
    freshness:
      warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour}
      error_after: {count: 12, period: hour}
    tables:
      - name: orders
        columns:
          - name: order_id
            tests: [not_null, unique]
          - name: amount
            tests:
              - dbt_utils.accepted_range:
                  min_value: 0
        tests:
          - dbt_utils.recency:
              datepart: hour
              field: loaded_at
              interval: 12
          - assert_row_count_within_pct:
              baseline: 7d_median
              tolerance_pct: 40  # partition <60% of median = alert
steps: Predict the downstream data-product decision before executing.
Freshness is a contract, not a hope: loaded_at_field + freshness turns 'is the source stale?' into a first-class check. This is the single signal the stale-revenue incident needed.
Two thresholds, two severities: warn_after 6h routes to Slack; error_after 12h pages on-call. Severity separates 'glance at this' from 'wake someone up' — noise-control at the threshold.

Schema + range tests on the source: not_null / unique / accepted_range catch a malformed partition (nulled IDs, negative amounts) at the source contract, before dbt propagates the corruption downstream.
Recency as a hard error: dbt_utils.recency fails the build if loaded_at is >12h old — so a stale source stops the metric instead of silently rebuilding it green.
Volume against a rolling baseline: A partition at <60% of the 7-day median is the classic truncated-feed signal a row-count-only test misses. Alert on the delta, not the absolute count.
Change one schema, freshness, ordering, retry, privacy, or cost assumption and name the evidence needed to catch the resulting false trust.

observability-alerting.subtitle: Source → ingestion → warehouse → dbt → metric. Five detectors tap the data path; each crosses a threshold into the alert router, which pages on-call with a runbook link. The failure path (stale source → green build → corrupted metric) is exactly what the freshness detector cuts.

storyboard.say: The pipeline runs left to right: a source feed delivers a partition to ingestion, which writes it to the warehouse.
The warehouse feeds dbt, which materializes the revenue metric the board actually reads.
Here is the failure: the source went stale on day one, the warehouse kept serving yesterday's partition, and dbt still built green.
No test failed, so the metric quietly reported 4.1 million to the board for six days while nobody watched freshness.
Detectors tap the data path: freshness, schema, and volume off the warehouse; quality and lineage off dbt.
When a detector crosses its numeric threshold, it fires into the alert router with a severity and a route.
The router pages on-call with a runbook link, so every alert names a next action instead of adding noise.
The core insight: the freshness detector cuts the exact stale-to-corrupt path, catching what green builds never will.

observability-alerting.text: DORA 2024 does not make claims about alerting practice, signal count, runbooks, or alert-to-action time. Rephrase without DORA attribution: 'Best-performing teams alert on fewer, sharper signals tied to a runbook and measure alert-to-action time.' The senior tell is a page you can act on half-asleep: 'orders_raw stale 30h → run backfill_runbook.md §3'. If your alert needs a Slack thread to figure out what it means, it is a symptom, not a signal.

observability-alerting.question: A reviewer asks: 'Prove this pipeline would have caught the stale-source incident, not just handled the happy path.' Which answer is the real evidence?
options: 'We added a Grafana dashboard showing daily row counts and revenue.'

'dbt source freshness has error_after: 12h on orders_raw; running it against the stale partition (loaded_at 30h old) trips the error, blocks the metric build, and pages on-call with backfill_runbook.md — here is the failing run output.'
'All our dbt tests pass and the build is green.'
'We log every ingestion event to the warehouse for later analysis.'
observability-alerting.explanation: Only option 2 points to the exact signal (freshness), the numeric threshold (12h), the failure output on a genuinely bad partition, and the resulting action (page + runbook) — the reviewer challenge from the source pack demands the broken case AND the proof output. A dashboard (1), a green build (3), and passive logs (4) all describe the happy path; none of them fire on the stale partition.

observability-alerting.title: Implement dbt-style freshness and volume-anomaly alerting
observability-alerting.summary: Complete two alerting functions — a source-freshness check (warn/error after N hours) and a row-count-within-percent-of-median volume check — then run the file in the browser to page on-call when either signal breaches its threshold. Match the exact observable data-product contract, retain a minimized failure as a regression, and identify the orchestration, warehouse, lineage, quality, privacy, cost, or production evidence still required. from statistics import median

# Daily row counts for the last 7 days of the `orders` partition.
BASELINE_ROW_COUNTS = [1000, 1200, 900, 1100, 1050, 950, 1150]

# Today's freshness + volume snapshot for the orders_raw source.
SNAPSHOT = {
    "hours_since_loaded": 8,   # how stale the newest data is
    "todays_row_count": 520,   # rows landed in today's partition
}

# Source freshness thresholds (from sources.yml)
FRESHNESS_WARN_AFTER_HOURS = 6
FRESHNESS_ERROR_AFTER_HOURS = 12

# Volume anomaly threshold: a partition under this % of the 7d median alerts.
VOLUME_MIN_PCT_OF_MEDIAN = 60


def freshness_status(hours_since_loaded):
    """Return 'error' if >= error threshold, 'warn' if >= warn threshold, else 'pass'."""
    # TODO: implement the freshness check using the two threshold constants.
    # Check the error threshold BEFORE the warn threshold (error is more severe).
    raise NotImplementedError


def volume_status(todays_row_count, baseline):
    """Return (median_of_baseline, pct_of_median, status).

    pct_of_median = todays_row_count / median(baseline) * 100
    status = 'alert' if pct_of_median < VOLUME_MIN_PCT_OF_MEDIAN else 'pass'
    """
    # TODO: compute the 7-day median, the percent-of-median, and the status.
    raise NotImplementedError


fresh = freshness_status(SNAPSHOT["hours_since_loaded"])
med, pct, vol = volume_status(SNAPSHOT["todays_row_count"], BASELINE_ROW_COUNTS)

print(f"freshness: {fresh}")
print(f"baseline_median: {med:.1f}")
print(f"volume_pct: {pct:.1f}")
print(f"volume: {vol}")

# Page on-call if EITHER the source is stale (warn/error) OR volume is anomalous.
alerting = fresh in ("warn", "error") or vol == "alert"
print(f"page_oncall: {alerting}")

cost-capacity.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'cost capacity under control' because a query is fast on dev data. Fast on 3 days is not bounded on 3 years. Without a partition-pruning budget and a freshness guard, the pipeline is one unpartitioned backfill away from a $9k warehouse bill and a stale metric shipped to the exec dashboard.

cost-capacity.text: The dbt run finished green, the daily-revenue tile updated, and everyone moved on — until finance found the number was 18 hours stale because the upstream orders extract silently stopped at 2 a.m., and a full-table backfill to 'fix' it scanned three years of partitions and burned the month's warehouse budget in one query.

Cost Capacity is the synthesis skill that binds a source contract, a freshness check, and lineage into one enforceable budget per pipeline run. It is Section 5 of the packet you carry through this module: the point where a stale partition or an unpruned scan is caught as a cost/quality failure before it becomes a wrong metric in front of a stakeholder.

cost-capacity.prompt: 'The nightly job runs in 90 seconds and costs pennies, so cost capacity is a non-issue.' Before you agree — what is wrong with using today's runtime as your capacity plan? Answer before reading on.
cost-capacity.reveal: It measures the happy path, not the blast radius. Runtime on one incremental partition tells you nothing about the day a schema drift forces a full refresh, a late-arriving backfill replays 1,000 partitions, or a missing WHERE clause turns an incremental model into a full-table scan. Cost capacity is not 'how much does a normal run cost' — it is 'what is the WORST a single run can cost, and what stops it before it corrupts the metric or the bill.' The invariant: every run has a bounded bytes-scanned budget and a freshness gate, or it has neither.

storyboard.say: It starts upstream: the orders extract lands raw rows as dated landing partitions in the store, one partition per day.
Every candidate partition is handed to the cost and freshness gate before any transform is allowed to touch it.
The gate enforces the source contract: a freshness SLA plus a per-run ceiling on partitions and warehouse-seconds scanned.
Stale or malformed input never reaches the model — the gate routes it straight to quarantine for inspection.
Only pruned, fresh partitions pass through to the dbt model, so a backfill can't silently scan three years of data.
dbt writes its rollup to the warehouse, which serves the daily revenue tile downstream.
The invariant: if budget or SLA fails, the gate blocks the metric outright — better a missing tile than an 18-hour-stale number.

ci-cd-data.text: The revenue dashboard reads $0 for the East region all morning. Nothing errored, every job was green, the deploy went out clean — an upstream feed silently stopped at 2 a.m. and the pipeline happily published the gap as truth. Code CI would never have caught it, because the code was fine. The data was not.

This is the synthesis lesson: it wires the whole course — source contracts, ingestion, dbt models, quality, lineage, reconciliation — into one gate that runs in CI/CD. It is what lets a data product deploy on a schedule without a human eyeballing every metric first.

ci-cd-data.prompt: Your dbt tests all pass in CI and the pipeline deploys. The next morning a key metric is wrong. How did green tests ship a broken number? Answer before reading on.
ci-cd-data.reveal: The tests validated the model, not the freshness or completeness of what fed it. dbt `not_null` and `unique` pass on an empty or stale partition — there are no nulls in rows that never arrived. CI/CD for DATA means the gate also asks: is the source fresh, does its schema match the contract, and does the output reconcile to the source row count? A pipeline that only tests transformation logic ships yesterday's data as today's with a green check.

ci-cd-data.code:
import sys, duckdb
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

con = duckdb.connect("warehouse.db")
FRESHNESS_SLA_MIN = 90          # source contract: max staleness

# 1. Schema check: contract columns must exist, types must match
expected = {"order_id": "BIGINT", "amount": "DECIMAL", "created_at": "TIMESTAMP"}
actual = dict(con.execute("DESCRIBE staging.orders").fetchall())
schema_ok = all(actual.get(c) == t for c, t in expected.items())

# 2. Freshness check: newest source row vs the SLA
newest = con.execute("SELECT max(created_at) FROM staging.orders").fetchone()[0]
fresh_ok = newest is not None and newest > datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(minutes=FRESHNESS_SLA_MIN)

# 3. Quarantine malformed rows instead of letting them into the metric
bad = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM staging.orders WHERE amount IS NULL OR amount < 0").fetchone()[0]
con.execute("INSERT INTO quarantine.orders SELECT * FROM staging.orders WHERE amount IS NULL OR amount < 0")

# 4. Reconciliation: does the modeled metric match the clean source count?
src = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM staging.orders WHERE amount >= 0").fetchone()[0]
metric = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM marts.daily_orders").fetchone()[0]
reconciled = src == metric

if not (schema_ok and fresh_ok and bad == 0 and reconciled):
    print(f"GATE FAILED schema={schema_ok} fresh={fresh_ok} quarantined={bad} reconciled={reconciled}")
    sys.exit(1)   # non-zero exit stops the deploy
print("GATE PASSED — promoting to warehouse")
steps: Predict the downstream data-product decision before executing.
The freshness SLA is the source contract: 90 minutes is a promise the source made. The gate enforces the promise; it is not a vibe about how old the data 'feels'.
Schema check against the contract: The expected column-to-type map IS the contract. If the source drops a column or changes a type, schema_ok is False before a single metric is computed.
Freshness kills the 2 a.m. silent-stall: The mission failure. If the newest row is older than the SLA, fresh_ok is False — the stale feed is caught here, not in the dashboard.
Quarantine, do not delete: Malformed rows are copied to a quarantine table so you have a bad-record report to inspect and repair — they never silently enter the metric.

Reconciliation is the anti-silent-loss check: Clean source rows must equal modeled rows. A mismatch means the transformation dropped data — the failure dbt tests cannot see because there are no nulls in rows that vanished.
Fail closed with a non-zero exit: sys.exit(1) is the whole point: CI treats non-zero as failure and stops the deploy. Fail-open (exit 0 with a warning) is how bad data ships.

legend.label: only a clean, reconciled run publishes

storyboard.say: A source feed lands a new partition and hands it to the CI/CD quality gate — this is where every deploy begins.
The gate doesn't trust the data blindly; it pulls the source contract and checks the partition against it.
Here's the decision: schema must match, data must be fresh, and the output must reconcile back to the source.
On failure — a stale or malformed partition — the gate fails closed and diverts the bad data into quarantine.
Only on pass does the gate release the partition to the dbt build downstream.
dbt produces a reconciled build and promotes it to the trusted warehouse metric — this is the only clean path out.
The repair loop: quarantined data triggers a backfill to fix the source, which re-enters the same gate.
The lesson: the gate proves the contract before deploy, so a silent upstream gap never reaches the dashboard as truth.

# 2. Freshness check: newest source row vs the SLA
newest = con.execute("SELECT max(created_at) FROM staging.orders").fetchone()[0]
fresh_ok = newest is not None and newest > datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(minutes=FRESHNESS_SLA_MIN)

# 3. Quarantine malformed rows instead of letting them into the metric
bad = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM staging.orders WHERE amount IS NULL OR amount < 0").fetchone()[0]
con.execute("INSERT INTO quarantine.orders SELECT * FROM staging.orders WHERE amount IS NULL OR amount < 0")

# 4. Reconciliation: does the modeled metric match the clean source count?
src = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM staging.orders WHERE amount >= 0").fetchone()[0]
metric = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM marts.daily_orders").fetchone()[0]
reconciled = src == metric

if not (schema_ok and fresh_ok and bad == 0 and reconciled):
    print(f"GATE FAILED schema={schema_ok} fresh={fresh_ok} quarantined={bad} reconciled={reconciled}")
    sys.exit(1)   # non-zero exit stops the deploy
print("GATE PASSED — promoting to warehouse")

steps.label: The freshness SLA is the source contract
steps.note: 90 minutes is a promise the source made. The gate enforces the promise; it is not a vibe about how old the data 'feels'.

steps.label: Schema check against the contract
steps.note: The expected column-to-type map IS the contract. If the source drops a column or changes a type, schema_ok is False before a single metric is computed.

steps.label: Freshness kills the 2 a.m. silent-stall
steps.note: The mission failure. If the newest row is older than the SLA, fresh_ok is False — the stale feed is caught here, not in the dashboard.

steps.label: Quarantine, do not delete
steps.note: Malformed rows are copied to a quarantine table so you have a bad-record report to inspect and repair — they never silently enter the metric.

steps.label: Reconciliation is the anti-silent-loss check
steps.note: Clean source rows must equal modeled rows. A mismatch means the transformation dropped data — the failure dbt tests cannot see because there are no nulls in rows that vanished.

steps.label: Fail closed with a non-zero exit
steps.note: sys.exit(1) is the whole point: CI treats non-zero as failure and stops the deploy. Fail-open (exit 0 with a warning) is how bad data ships.

incident-response.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'handled the incident' if your only action was re-running the pipeline until the number looked right. incident-response.text: Monday 8 a.m.: the exec revenue dashboard reads $0 for Saturday, and it has been wrong all weekend because a vendor silently shipped a CSV with a renamed column. Nobody was paged, because nothing was watching the source contract — the pipeline ran green on garbage the whole time.

This is the synthesis lesson of the course: it fuses source contracts, freshness, quarantine, lineage, and reconciliation into one drill you run under fire. Incident response is where every earlier skill either holds or fails — Section 'Incident Response' of the packet you carry into the capstone.

incident-response.prompt: A downstream metric is wrong. Your first instinct is to re-run the pipeline. Before you do — what does a green re-run actually prove? Answer before reading on.
incident-response.reveal: Almost nothing. If the source data is stale or malformed, the pipeline will happily re-run and produce the same wrong number, still green — success just means 'no code exception', not 'data is correct'. The real first move is to isolate: which partition, which source, which contract assertion should have failed and didn't. You quarantine the bad records and reconcile the metric before you touch the pipeline, because re-running is the one action that can overwrite your only evidence of what broke.

## Incident Response — 2026-07-01 · revenue_daily wrong
- Detection: dbt source freshness on `vendor.orders` — max(loaded_at) 61h > 24h SLA (WARN missed; renamed col passed schema)
- Lineage (source -> metric): vendor.orders -> stg_orders -> fct_orders -> revenue_daily -> exec_dashboard.revenue
- Blast radius: revenue_daily partitions 2026-06-28..30 (3 days); no data loss, values understated ~100%
- Quarantine: 14,204 rows where amount IS NULL routed to vendor.orders__quarantine (renamed `amount`->`gross_amt`)
- Reconcile: revenue_daily(2026-06-29) = $0 -> $148,912 after remap; matches Stripe payouts ledger (source of truth)
- Contract change: add not_null(amount) + column-presence test on `amount`; freshness WARN -> ERROR (block + page)
- Reversal condition: if remap misstates > 0.5% vs Stripe, roll back mart + reindex from raw off-hours
steps: Predict the downstream data-product decision before executing.
Detection signal: Name the exact check that caught it (freshness) AND the one that missed it (schema passed because the column was renamed, not dropped). The gap is the lesson.
Lineage trace: Walk the graph from the failed source to the corrupted metric, node by node. Without lineage you are guessing at blast radius.
Blast radius: Which partitions, how bad, and — critically — understated vs lost. Stale-and-recoverable is a different incident than data-loss.
Quarantine: Isolate the bad rows to a __quarantine table with the root cause (renamed column). Never delete evidence; a re-run would overwrite it.
Reconciliation: The metric before ($0) and after ($148,912), tied to an independent source of truth (Stripe payouts). This is the proof, not the re-run.
Harden + reversal: A not_null test plus a column-presence contract and freshness escalated to ERROR — so the next silent rename pages you. Plus the condition that reverses the fix.
Change one schema, freshness, ordering, retry, privacy, or cost assumption and name the evidence needed to catch the resulting false trust.

storyboard.say: Monday 8 a.m.: a vendor silently ships a CSV with a renamed column. The bad partition lands at the contract gate.
Nobody was watching the source contract, so the gate waves the garbage through — a silent pass, and that is the bug.
The bad rows land in the warehouse and corrupt the revenue metric. The dashboard reads $0, green the whole weekend.
The fix: the contract gate should have routed that partition into quarantine instead of into the warehouse.
Now you reconcile — diff the corrupted metric against truth, then replay the clean partition out of quarantine.
From the incident you write a hardened assertion that prevents this exact recurrence.
That assertion arms the gate: next time this vendor breaks the schema, it pages you instead of shipping silently.

data-capstone.prompt: Your dbt run is green, all tests pass, the freshness macro is happy — and the daily revenue metric is still wrong. How is that possible? Answer before reading on.
data-capstone.reveal: Because a green pipeline only proves the transforms ran, not that the INPUT was correct. If the source landed a partition late, or a partner silently dropped a currency column to null, the model faithfully computes a wrong number from wrong-but-well-typed data. The invariant of a data product: the contract and freshness gate must fail at the SOURCE boundary, before the DAG ever transforms it — and a reconciliation must tie the published metric back to the source of truth. Schema-valid is not the same as correct.

# data_contract_quality_and_lineage_packet.md  (excerpt: models/staging/_partner_sales.yml)
version: 2
sources:
  - name: partner_sales
    freshness:                       # freshness SLA — fail if source is stale
      warn_after:  { count: 2, period: hour }
      error_after: { count: 4, period: hour }
    loaded_at_field: _ingested_at
    tables:
      - name: orders
        columns:
          - name: order_id
            tests: [not_null, unique]          # schema check: key integrity
          - name: amount_usd
            tests:
              - not_null                       # malformed row -> quarantine
              - dbt_utils.accepted_range: { min_value: 0 }
          - name: region
            tests:
              - accepted_values: { values: ['NE','SE','MW','W'] }

# Quality gate (models/staging/stg_orders.sql) — route bad rows out, don't drop the run
select *,
  case when amount_usd is null or region not in ('NE','SE','MW','W')
       then true else false end as _quarantined
from {{ source('partner_sales','orders') }}
steps: Predict the downstream data-product decision before executing.

Freshness SLA (the late-partition catch): loaded_at_field + error_after: 4h is the check that would have caught the six-hour-late Northeast partition. Without it, the DAG happily transforms stale data into a wrong metric.
Schema check on the key: not_null + unique on order_id is the source contract's spine — a duplicated or missing key corrupts every downstream aggregation.
Malformed-value contract: amount_usd not_null + accepted_range(min 0) rejects the silent null-currency drop and negative-amount corruption before they reach the mart.
Accepted-values on region: the partition that arrives with region='NORTHEAST' instead of 'NE' fails here — lineage will show this is exactly the column that zeroed the dashboard.
Quarantine, don't drop: the gold move: flag bad rows into _quarantined so they land in the report instead of vanishing. A dropped row is invisible data loss; a quarantined row is evidence.

storyboard.say: A partner source lands a partition — but instead of trusting it, the packet routes it straight into a contract gate at the boundary.
The gate is the decision point: it checks freshness and shape before a single row goes downstream. This is where the six-hour-late partition dies.
Stale or malformed rows never reach the pipeline — they divert to quarantine, the repair path, where bad records wait for inspection instead of poisoning the metric.
Only rows that pass the contract are accepted into Raw Bronze — the transform stage sees clean, on-time data by construction.
The dbt model transforms accepted data and publishes the revenue metric — every column traceable back to a source that cleared the gate.
The published metric doesn't stand alone — reconciliation compares it against the numbers and flags any drift.
Reconciliation ties the metric back to the source of truth, closing the loop — so a silent $0 becomes a caught, explained failure.

# The lesson defined a dbt source contract for `orders`:

data-capstone.question: Hollow pipeline vs a real data product

optionA.label: Hollow: happy-path only
optionA.text: Ingests whatever lands — no freshness SLA · dbt tests exist but only not_null on one column · Bad rows silently dropped, no quarantine report · No lineage: nobody knows region feeds revenue · No reconciliation to source of truth · Dashboard reads $0 NE; found by a customer Outcome: Green DAG, corrupted metric, silent for 6h

optionB.label: Real: contract + quality + lineage + recon
optionB.text: Freshness error_after 4h fails the stale partition · Schema + accepted-values contract at the boundary · Bad rows quarantined into an inspectable report · Lineage maps source.region → stg → revenue_by_region · Reconciliation ties metric to source-of-truth totals · Pipeline halts + alerts BEFORE publishing a wrong number Outcome: Bad data stopped at the door, with evidence

data-capstone.guidance: The difference is not more code — it is the evidence. The real product can PROVE it caught the failure; the hollow one only proves rows moved. Defend correctness, freshness, idempotency, recoverability, observability, governance, latency, and cost with evidence.

data-capstone.intro: Prove the packet is a data product, not a note — run every check:
items: Schema check: `dbt build` fails when order_id is duplicated or amount_usd is null. If it passes on malformed input, your contract is decoration.
Freshness check: `dbt source freshness` errors when the partition is >4h stale. Simulate a late load and confirm the gate fires before transform.
Lineage map: you can trace source.partner_sales.region → stg_orders.region → revenue_by_region.amount in the packet, so the reviewer sees which column zeroed the metric.
Quarantine report: the bad-record report lists the rejected rows with the reason (null amount / bad region), not a silent row-count drop.
Metric reconciliation: the published revenue for the partition ties out to the source-of-truth total within tolerance; a mismatch blocks the publish.

prompts: Roll-call the course: name the section of this packet that each skill produced — source contract, ingestion, orchestration, dbt model, data quality, reconciliation, lineage, backfill, streaming, governance, observability.
Explain, using your own packet, why a green DAG is not proof a metric is correct — and which two checks (freshness + reconciliation) close that gap.
Walk the failure autopsy: trace the late/malformed partition from source through the contract gate to the quarantine report, then say the reusable repair rule it earned.
